1.title: Increment and Definition of Done
1.text: Welcome to Module 12: Increment and Definition of Done. This completes the three artifacts. You will learn what an Increment is, how several can appear in one Sprint, what the Definition of Done commits the team to, and how to build and strengthen one. These ideas also protect you from the almost-done trap.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. State the purpose and attributes of the Increment. Explain how several Increments can arise in one Sprint. Explain the Definition of Done as the commitment of the Increment. Give three advantages of a strong one, and one way to create it. Explain how it evolves, and why teams on one product share it. And spot the traps: almost done, relaxing it, and treating the Review as a gate.

1.title: Case Check-In: Defects at the Stations
1.text: At RideLoop, Lena reports that defects keep reaching the test stations. The kiosk firmware tests are manual, and they get skipped when time is short. The team's Definition of Done has five lines, and none of them mentions those tests. As Scrum Master, you ask what Done should really mean for this product. By the end of the module, you will have a method for answering that.

1.title: The Increment
1.text: An Increment is a usable step toward the Product Goal. It is additive to all earlier Increments, and it is thoroughly verified, so that all the Increments work together. The Guide puts the birth moment very simply: "The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born." An item that misses the Definition of Done does not become part of an Increment. It returns to the Product Backlog.

1.title: Attributes of an Increment
1.text: The learning objective asks for attributes of the Increment. It is a step toward the Product Goal. It is additive, building on every earlier Increment. It is thoroughly verified, checked so that all the Increments work together. It must be usable to provide value. It meets the Definition of Done: no Definition of Done met, no Increment. And it is inspectable, because the total of all the Increments is shown at the Sprint Review. Name any three.

1.title: Several Increments in a Sprint
1.text: How many Increments can a Sprint produce? Several. Each time an item meets the Definition of Done, a new Increment exists and is added to the earlier ones. The total of them is shown at the Sprint Review. But an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders earlier than that. The Review is never a gate to releasing value. In the earlier edition, you will find potentially releasable, and a single Increment at the end of the Sprint.

1.title: The Definition of Done
1.text: The Definition of Done is the formal statement of the condition the Increment must reach, in terms of the quality measures the product needs. It is the commitment of the Increment. It creates transparency, because everyone shares an understanding of what was completed. And if an item misses it, the item cannot be released or even shown at the Review. It goes back to the Product Backlog. Almost done is not Done.

1.title: Whose Definition, and Which Standard
1.text: Whose is it, and which standard applies? The Developers are required to conform to it. If the organization has a standard, every Scrum Team follows it as a minimum, and may add to it. If no standard exists, the Scrum Team creates one that suits the product. And when several teams work on one product, they define and follow the same Definition of Done together. Neither the Scrum Master nor the Product Owner relaxes it to meet a date.

1.title: Advantages of a Strong Definition of Done
1.text: The learning objective asks for at least three advantages of a strong Definition of Done. These go beyond the Guide. A shared understanding of what Done means. Built-in quality, so quality does not decrease. Less rework, because defects are caught before an item is Done. Less technical debt, because shortcuts are not accepted as Done. Better forecasts, because the Developers know what each item takes. Release readiness: a usable Increment can go out at any time. And trust, because stakeholders can rely on what they see at the Review.

1.title: Creating a Definition of Done
1.text: How do you create a Definition of Done? The Guide says who does it, but not how, so this method goes beyond the Guide. First, collect the organization's standards: that is the minimum. Second, identify the quality the product needs, such as testing, security and deployment. Third, select criteria that are verifiable and apply to every item. Fourth, agree on them and make them visible. Fifth, apply them to every item. Sixth, strengthen them in Retrospectives. If a question asks for one way, this is a good one to give.

1.title: Example: The RideLoop Definition of Done
1.text: Here is RideLoop's. It is an example from the case, not Guide text. Today it has five lines: code reviewed by a second Developer, tests passing on both phone platforms, an accessibility check, deployment to the test stations, and no known critical defect. After the defects at the stations, the team considers adding two candidates: the kiosk firmware tests are run, not skipped, and the unlock flow is tested on a crowded-station network profile. Notice that each criterion is a yes or no.

1.title: How a Definition of Done Evolves
1.text: How does a Definition of Done evolve? It is a living agreement. It is strengthened over time, not relaxed. The triggers are lessons from Retrospectives, defects that escaped, new tooling, new standards, and a growing product. A stronger definition can even reveal work missing from items that were called Done earlier. The earlier edition expected definitions to expand as teams mature. So when defects escape, the answer is to strengthen it. The Retrospective is where the team inspects it and improves it. The Guide mentions the Retrospective inspecting the Definition of Done, but says nothing about how it evolves, so this goes beyond it.

1.title: Several Teams, One Definition of Done
1.text: Why do several Scrum Teams on one product share one Definition of Done? These reasons go beyond the Guide, and the objective asks for at least two. Different standards would not fit together, so the Increment would not be integrated. Quality stays consistent across the product. Stakeholders get shared transparency about what Done means. And a weaker standard in one team would hide unfinished work that surfaces later.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. Done means the Definition of Done is met; almost done is not Done. An item that does not meet it is not presented, not released, and goes back to the Product Backlog. The Developers conform, and nobody relaxes it to meet a date. The organization's standard comes first, as a minimum; otherwise the Scrum Team creates one. An Increment must be usable, and may be delivered before the Review. And there is no hardening Sprint: quality is built into every item.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. An Increment is usable, additive, and thoroughly verified. It is born when an item meets the Definition of Done. Several can appear in one Sprint, and the Review is not a gate. The Definition of Done is the commitment of the Increment, and it gives a shared understanding. A strong one brings quality, less rework and less debt, and trust. It evolves stronger, and teams on one product share it. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A RideLoop Developer finishes an item on day three that meets the Definition of Done. Maya wants to wait until the Sprint Review to release it. What does the Guide say? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. An Increment may be delivered before the end of the Sprint, and the Review is never a gate to releasing value. The Review is for inspection, not for permission.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Lakeshore Transit has a security standard that all products must meet. The RideLoop team wants a weaker Definition of Done to move faster. What is the answer? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. When the Definition of Done is part of the organization's standards, every Scrum Team follows it as a minimum. A team may add criteria to suit its product, but may not weaken it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Three Scrum Teams work on one Lakeshore Transit product, each with its own Definition of Done, and integration problems appear every Sprint. What should the Scrum Master advise? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. The teams should agree one Definition of Done together and all follow it, so that every Increment works together. A hardening Sprint is not part of Scrum.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which is an advantage of a strong Definition of Done? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. It gives everyone a shared understanding of what is complete and builds quality into every item. It does not remove the need for Retrospectives, and it adds no approval gate for the Scrum Master.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which is a sound way to create a Definition of Done? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Start from the organization's standards as the minimum, then let the Scrum Team select verifiable criteria that suit the product. Make them visible, apply them to every item, and strengthen them in Retrospectives.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. An Increment may be delivered early. Question two: D. The organization's standard is the minimum. Question three: C. Teams on one product share one Definition of Done. Question four: B. Shared understanding and built-in quality. Question five: A. Standards first, then verifiable criteria. That completes Module 12. Next, Module 13 covers facilitation, teaching, mentoring and coaching.
